title: Helping a team adopt AI, and proving it with evidence

say: Helping a team adopt AI, and proving it with evidence.
This is the video for module three of AI Productivity Systems.

When a team asks for help using AI, the request is usually vague. If you jump straight to prompt training, nothing sticks. So you start with discovery: a short investigation of how the work really flows.

panel.heading: Take your system beyond yourself
items: Find where a team's time really goes
Price a coaching engagement honestly
Lead adoption with a shared playbook
Present your results as a case study

say: Then you price the work, help the team adopt it, and turn the results into evidence for your portfolio.

say: Bisi coaches a six-person delivery business in Ibadan. Two staff spend 75 minutes a day, six days a week, answering customers about delivery status. That is 900 minutes a week.

panel.heading: Bisi's discovery at a dispatch business
items: Status replies: 900 minutes a week
End-of-day summary: 240 minutes a week
Payment reminders: 90 minutes a week
Total: 1,230 minutes, 20.5 hours a week

say: The owner's daily summary takes 240 minutes a week, and payment reminders 90.

say: Status replies contain customer names and addresses, so she uses saved reply templates instead. And payment amounts come from the accounts sheet, with the owner approving the wording.
Sometimes discovery shows a simple template or tidy-up is the first fix, not AI. Say so plainly.

say: A workshop teaches ideas. It suits teams that only need the concepts.

panel.heading: Workshop or build-and-coach
right: Higher fee, more of your time

say: But habits take weeks to form. A six-week build-and-coach engagement builds and tests routines with the team, and the log shows measured results.

say: Bisi estimates hours for each stage: discovery, building the routines, training, six weekly check-ins, and the final review. That adds up to 33 hours.

say: Half, 190,000 naira, is paid on signing and half on handover, with a receipt for every payment.
If the owner wants a lower price, she removes a stage instead of cutting her rate. And she never promises a fixed number of hours saved. She promises to measure.

say: A team system must survive holidays and staff changes, so write it down in a shared playbook.

Pick one willing person as a routine champion. People adopt what they see a trusted colleague using. And when someone worries that AI will make mistakes in their name, point to the review gate: nothing leaves without a human check.

panel.heading: The team AI playbook
items: Shared context file and dated facts sheet
Prompt library, with date last tested
Routine cards, each with an owner and a backup
Approved tools list
AI use rules: what never goes in, who reviews
A 20-minute monthly look at the log

say: Before measuring time saved, check that routines are actually being run.

panel.heading: Is the team really running the routines?
items: Run rate = completed runs / scheduled runs
Six weeks: 40 of 48 runs completed
Run rate: 83 percent
Payment reminders: only 4 of 6
Fix: move the trigger from Saturday to Thursday

say: Over six weeks, the dispatch business completed 40 of 48 scheduled runs. That is 83 percent.

say: Payment reminders were weakest. Staff explained they fell on Saturday, their busiest day. So the owner moved them to Thursday. A low run rate usually has a simple fix.

say: Evidence beats claims. Show where you started, what you built, and what your log measured.

panel.heading: An honest case study in five parts
items: Starting point and before timings
What you built, with one routine card
Measured result: minutes, run rate, errors
What did not work, and why
What changed next

say: Include what did not work. It shows judgement and makes the rest believable.
Ask permission before naming a client or sharing their figures, and hide customer details in screenshots.

say: To remember. Start with discovery. Cost by stage, with contingency. Keep accounts in the client's name and data rules in writing. Check the run rate first. And tell the whole story in your case study.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Discovery first: diaries, interviews, real samples
Cost by stage, plus 10 to 20 percent contingency
The client owns the accounts; data rules in writing
Fix a low run rate before measuring savings
Case studies include what did not work

say: Prove the system on yourself first, then help one other person, then package the evidence.
